OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing away of Shri 
Vedprakash P. Goyal, a former Member of this House, on the 17th December, 2008, at the age of 82. 
Born at Karnal in Haryana in January, 1926, Shri Goyal had his education at Dayanand Anglo 
Vedic College, Lahore (now in Pakistan) and in Banaras Hindu University. 
An industrialist, Shri Goyal was associated with several social and cultural organisations. Shri 
Goyal was an expert in the field of design, development and import substitution of capital equipment. 
He was former Chairman of Pradeep Metals Ltd. Mumbai, Janakalyan Sahakari Bank Ltd., Mumbai, 
and Maharashtra State Finance Corporation. He worked for the empowerment of women, 
development of slums and upliftment of Adivasis through "Friends of Tribal Society", especially in 
the field of education, health and sanitation. He was also founder Editor of Nirbhay Pathik, a Hindi 
daily published from Mumbai. 
Shri Goyal represented the State of Maharashtra in this House from 3rd April, 1996, to 2nd 
April, 2002, and again from 3rd April, 2002, to 2nd April, 2008. He also served as the Chairman of the 
House Committee^ from March, 2000 to September, 2001. He was also the Minister of Shipping in 
the Union Council of Ministers from September, 2001, to January, 2003. 
In the passing away of Shri Vedprakash P. Goyal, the country has lost a distinguished 
parliamentarian and an able administrator. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Vedprakash P. Goyal. 
I request hon. Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect to the 
memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the bereaved family our 
deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

Optimum use of Raw Materials 
*261.  SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI:†† 
     DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
†† The questioni was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Greesh Kumar Sangi. 

2 
(a) whether experts on steel feel that every ounce of raw materials, such as iron-ore, coal and 
manganese whose prices are touching all time high, should be used properly; 
(b) if so, whether utilisation of every ounce of these raw materials is of fundamental importance 
as they play a very important role in the strategy of a company; 
(c) whether steel companies have been urged to make optimum use of raw materials so that 
steel industry works well; 
(d) if so, to what extent efforts in this regard have been taken by them; and 
(e) to what extent results have been achieved? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZER S AND THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. In order to ensure sustainable growth/development of iron & steel sector 
and also to ensure cost competitiveness, it is im perative for the Indian steel industry to optimally 
utilize raw materials like iron ore, coal, mangan ese ore etc. The prices of iron ore, coal and 
manganese ore after touching very high levels during earlier part of the year have recently come 
down. 
(c) Policies of Government emphasis on scientific methods of mining, beneficiation & 
agglomeration and economic utilization of low grade ores and rejects. Government is also 
encouraging Research and Development (R&D) efforts in the area of development of innovative/ 
path breaking technology for utilizing iron ore fines and Non-Coking Coal in steel making and 
beneficiation of coking/ non-coking coal with improved yield. 
(d) and (e) Various measures are being undertaken by domestic iron & steel industry for 
optimum utilization of raw materials resultin g in increased cost competitiveness, which inter-alia 
include the following: 
• Setting up beneficiation, sintering and palletizatio n plants for optimum utilization of iron ore fines 
and low grade iron ore & setting up beneficiation plants for up-gradation and optimum utilization 
of low grade manganese ore. 
• Introduction of new technologies to optimize util ization of coking coal and to replace coking coal 
by non-coking coal. 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Sir, the answer  given to the question does not mention 
anything very specifically as to what research and development programmes are there, as to how 
much the Government would spend on this research and development to improve the material 
balancing and utilisation of raw material used in steel industry. Steel and cement are the two major 
components of the development of the country and infrastructure in our country, and it is very 
pathetic that our country is exporting iron ore to the tune of almost about hundred million tonnes, 
which is almost double the quantity of steel we produce. The need of the hour is to see that we utilise 
the fines and low-grade iron also. There is also an urgent need to start research and development 
activities and to bring in new technology to utilise the non-coking coal also. 
I would like to know from the hon. Minister, through you, Sir, as to what specifically we are trying 
to do in this regard. The consumpt ion of steel in our country is 2 kgs. per person, per annum. It is 
very low when compared to the global market.

*262. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether competent authority is aware that many students of scheduled caste and 
scheduled tribe category are deprived of admission to MBBS course in various medical colleges 
since they did not receive qualifying marks prescribed by the Medical Council of India(MCI) for 
entrance examination; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that many seats are no t filled with SC/ST candidates due to the above 
instruction of MCI; 

6 
(d) if so, whether steps will be taken to fill the seats considering the marks received in the 
qualifying examination and the entrance examination as parameters; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (e) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
In the Medical Council of India, Graduate Medi cal Education Regulations 1997, as approved by 
the Central Government, relaxation has been provided  in criteria for admission to MBBS course, in 
respect of SC/ST students. While 50% of marks have been prescribed for General category 
candidates for qualifying examination as well as entrance examination, it is 40% of marks for 
candidates belonging to SC/ST categories. 
The MBBS seats are filled up under two categories namely "All India Quota" and "State Quota". 
Under All India quota, 15% MBBS seats of the State are contributed by the respective State 
Government. In so far as admission of SC and ST students in the All India quota is concerned, 
reservation at the rate of 15% and 7-1/2% respectively has been introduced from the academic year 
2008-09. As per information available for the academic year 2008-09, against 329 total seats for SC 
students, there was no shortfall. As regard ST students, against 164 total seats for ST students, 111 
ST candidates were allotted. Thus, there has been some shortfall of ST candidates. 
With regard to State Quota for the remaining 85% seats, the admission process is conducted by 
the respective State Government. As such the Central Government does not maintain any data in the 
matter. While the State Governments have not pointed out any problem of shortage of filling up of 
SC/ST MBBS seats in the State, in the recent past the Government of Kerala informed the Central 
Government that ST candidates of their State are no t able to qualify in the entrance examination for 
getting admission against the reserved seats due to the above mentioned MCI norms. In the 
meanwhile, a Civil Writ Petition No. 393/2008 - Vineeth K. and others versus S t a t e  o f  K e r a l a  a n d  
others - has also been filed in the Hon'ble Supreme Court challenging the criteria of 40% marks for 
ST/SC students. The Hon'ble Court taking a note of the shortfall, has issued notices to Union of 
India and eight other States viz. Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Orissa, West Bengal, U.P., M.P. 
and Karnataka. The matter is sub-judice.

*263. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a ship 'SS Oceanic' carrying 250 tonnes of asbestos, a toxic 
material, was headed for Alang in Saurashtra coast;

handling of toxic waste from dismantled ships; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government has taken on both the counts? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILISERS AND THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The concerned agencies have reported that they have no information about the possible 
arrival of the ship 'SS Oceanic' at Alang on the Saurashtra coast. 
(b) and (c) A series of measures have been taken for attenuating the hazards of ship breaking 
and for improving the working conditions at shipbreaking yards at Alang. The Hon'ble Supreme Court 
of  India  has  also issued comprehensive directives in this matter. Consequently, detailed protocols  

11 
and procedures have been put in place for scrutinizing ships arriving for breaking and for handling 
and disposing of hazardous materials and wastes. The concerned nodal agency, the Gujarat 
Maritime Board has also developed a Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility, (TSDF) for treatment

Gujarat State Pollution Control Board also monitors the handling of hazardous waste.

Heavy metals in ayurvedic medicines 
*264. DR. JANARDHAN WAGHMARE:†† 
 SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the American drug regulator, Food and Drug Administration (FDA), has recently 
revised and issued its import alert following recent findings that ayurvedic drugs shipped from India 
contained high level of toxic heavy metals; 
(b) if so, the facts thereof and the details of the companies and names of the ayurvedic drugs 
to which Government have allowed export and were found to contain detectable levels of heavy 
metals; and 
(c) the steps Government proposes to take to ban manufacture/ sale / export of such 
ayurvedic drugs which contain toxic heavy metals? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFAR E (DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Website of the US Food and Drug Admi nistration (US.FDA) states that "Ayurvedic 
products are generally not reviewed or approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)". 
However, the US.FDA has urged the consumers to use caution with Ayurvedic products due to the 
presence of metal containing products exceeding perm issible limits found in them, in the wake of an 
article published in the August 27th, 2008, issue of  the Journal of the American Medical Association 
(JAMA) which stated that 1/5th of the US manufactured and Indian manufactured Ayurvedic 
products bought through websites on the internet  contain detectable level of lead, mercury or 
arsenic. 
(b) An internet search using 5 internet search engines and the search terms 'Ayurveda and 
Ayurvedic Medicine' identified 25 websites offering / selling Ayurvedic products. From the 673 
identified Ayurvedic products, 230 medicines were randomly selected for purchase between August - 
October, 2005 and orders placed for their purchase. However, the researchers received only 193 
products which were subjected to an analysis using x-ray, fluorescence, spectroscopy and nearly 
21% of these products were found to contain detectable levels of lead, mercury or arsenic. 
†† The questioni was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Janardhan Waghmare. 

15 
As per this article, detectable levels of lead, mercury or arsenic were found in the following Indian 
manufactured Ayurvedic products: 
S.No. Name of Indian Company Name of Products 
1. Goodcare Pharma Ezi Slim 
2. Baidyanath Ekangvir Ras, Agnitundi Bati, Brahmi,  
  Amoebica, Arogyavardhini Bati 
3. Maharishi Ayurved Vital Lady, Worry Free 
4. Sharangdhar Ayu-Arthri-Tone, 
 Pharmaceuticals Ayu-Hemoridi-Tone, Ayu-Leuko-Tone,  
  Ayu-Niphro-Tone 
This study followed a previous study published in JAMA on December 15, 2004, which found that 
one out of five Ayurvedic 'herbal medicine products' produced in South Asia and available in South 
Asian grocery stores in Boston contained potentially harmful levels of lead, mercury, and/or arsenic. 
(c) The Government have taken immediate steps to test the samples appearing in Journal of 
the American Medical Association (JAMA) article from reputed National Accreditation Board of 
Laboratories (NABL) accredited laboratories. The Central Council for Research in Ayurveda and 
Siddha (CCRAS) has undertaken a study to see the toxicity/safety profile of metal based bhasmas. 
The study is being carried out in Indian Toxicological  Research Center (ITRC), Council for Scientific 
and Industrial Research (CSIR), Lucknow. Pharmacopoeial Laboratory of Indian Medicine (PLIM), 
Ghaziabad has been directed to procure samples of  all the products mentioned in both the JAMA 
articles and send them to Indian Institute of Chemical Technology (IICT), Hyderabad for heavy metal 
analysis by electron spectroscopic chemical analysis as well as X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. 
The manufacturers of Ayurvedic medicines mentioned in JAMA articles have been directed to get 
safety/toxicity studies carried out for their products by National Accreditation Board of Laboratories / 
Good Laboratories Practices (NABL/GLP) accredited laboratories and send their report in respect of 
acute, sub acute and chronic safety/toxicity drug studies. After examination it was found that no 
Indian exported herbal ayurvedic medicine contained toxic heavy metals more than the permissible 
limit. As far as purely herbal Ayurvedic formulations are concerned, presence of heavy metals was 
not detected. As regards herbo-mineral and herbo-metallic preparations, metals are an essential 
ingredient of these formulations and, therefore, are bound to be present in these, however they are 
permitted to be used only after due purification and only in small quantities to act as catalysts for 
activation of other herbal ingredients in order to increase the efficacy of the medicines. The metallic 
preparations in the form of compounds of metals triturated in the form of 'Bhasmas' are rendered 
safe after purification with herbs and burning in fire for a prescribed number of times. 
Further, a Press release was issued on 2nd September, 2008 with detailed comments by the 
Department of AYUSH to counter the article publishe d in JAMA. The following orders have also been 
issued by the Central Government to ensure safety and efficacy of AYUSH products in the country 
and abroad: - 

16 
i) Government has introduced mandatory testing fo r heavy metals in all purely herbal Ayurveda, 
Siddha and Unani medicines to be exported with effect from 01.01.06 onwards. This has been 
done to meet the regulatory requirements of importing countries. 
ii) State Drug Licensing Authorities have been directed to ensure full compliance by all ASU drug 
manufacturers of the provisions of Rule 161 (1) and (2) relating to displaying on the label of the 
container or in a leaflet to be inserted in the package of an ASU drug, the true list of all the 
ingredients used in the manufacture of the preparation together with the quantity of each of the 
ingredients incorporated therein. 
iii) A research project has been sanctioned to various laboratories of Council of Scientific and 
Industrial Research (CSIR) under the Golden  Triangle Partnership Project to study the 
physiochemical characteristics of 8 most widely used Bhasmas and to carry out their toxicity 
studies. 
iv) Good Manufacturing Practices have been made mandatory for all Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani 
drug manufacturing units in the country. 
v) Department of AYUSH has discussed with Minister of Commerce to set up an AYUSH Export 
Promotion Council under the Department of AYUSH to take care of critical issues like testing 
and certification of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani medicines for export. 
vi) Government have constituted Pharmacopoeia Committees of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani 
systems of medicines for preparation of Pharmacopoeias to ensure the quality of Ayurveda, 
Siddha and Unani drugs. 
vii) Captain Shreeniwas Murti Drug Research Institute for Ayurveda, Chennai, IITR, Lucknow and 
Sri Ram Institute for Industrial Research, New Delhi, have analyzed about 600 plants and it was 
found that lead arsenic and mercury levels were within the permissible limits. 
viii) State Licensing Authorities have been direct ed to constitute an Expert Committee under the 
provision of Rule 154 (2) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rule, 1945, for streamlining the system 
for licensing of patent and proprietary Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani products.

allopathic drugs. For others, they just give advice. I understand that there have been some issues 
about the articles written in Boston and other areas where it was mentioned that Indian drugs or 
Ayurvedic drugs have heavy metals or metallic components and all that. They are drugs in India. In 
the USA they are food supplements. They are not drugs. They do not undergo any process there. 
So, it is the onus of the importing country also to s ee what all is there. Also, we have tested a lot of 
these drugs and found a majority of them have a permissible WHO level of metal components. So, 
there are different types of permissible levels for a drug and a food item. It is a complex issue. 
Nevertheless, I would like to reassure the hon. Member and agree with him that all the ingredients 
have to be mentioned on all the packets which are being sold in these units.

drugs. There are cases that we have also tested a lot of these drugs ourselves and found that most 
of these drugs have the permissible levels. Nevertheless, the institutions that do not have or the units 
which manufacture drugs which have higher than the permissible levels of metals, etc., we have sent 
notices and they have been closed. We have given the responsibility to the State authorities and we 
are also trying to set up infrastructure and a drug testing lab. 
Apart from this, a number of studies have also been carried out. A concept called the Golden

Pregnancy related deaths 
*266. SHRI B. J. PANDA: 
 MS. MABEL REBELLO: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that half a million of women die during child-birth, of whom 
70,000 are from India, in other words a woman dies every six minutes from a pregnancy-related 
cause in India, as per a new survey conducted by an NGO "The White Ribbon Alliance India"; 
(b) whether Government is also aware that a coun try's maternal mortality rate is considered to 
be the best indicator of its health system; and 
(c) if so, what is the action plan of Governme nt to control the high rate of woman mortality 
during child-birth? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFAR E (DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) 
The Registrar General of India, Ministry of Home Af fairs, brings out estimates of maternal mortality 
through its Sample Registration System. As per the latest survey report titled "Maternal Mortality in 
India: 1997-2003 trends, causes and risk factors" published in the year 2006 by the Registrar General 
of India, nearly 78,000 maternal deaths have been es timated on the basis of about 26 million births in 
2004. It has been ascertained from the NGO "The White Ribbon Alliance India" that they have not 
conducted any such survey. 
For a holistic appreciation of the status of health care, several morbidity and mortality indicators 
are relevant and required to be monitored, including Maternal Mortality Ratio. 
In this context, the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) was launched in April, 2005, to 
improve access to equitable, affordable, accountable and effective primary health care, especially in 
the rural areas of the country, particularly for poor women and children, with special focus on 18 
States which have weak public health indicators and weak infrastructure. Under the Mission, the 
following key strategies and interventions are being implemented to accelerate the pace of reduction 
in maternal mortality, namely: 
• Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), a cash benefit scheme to promote Institutional Delivery with a 
special focus on Below Poverty Line (BPL) and SC/ST pregnant women; 

22 
• The recently conducted District Level Household Survey (DLHS-III) has shown increase in 
institutional deliveries in most States. Kerala has shown 99.4% institutional delivery, Puducherry 
has shown 99.1% institutional delivery and Chandigarh has shown an increase of 28.7% points 
in institutional deliveries over the previous DL HS-II survey. Even States with low institutional 
delivery rates have shown increase in institutional deliveries. For example, in Madhya Pradesh, 
institutional deliveries have increased by 18.85% points and in Rajasthan this increase is 15.2% 
points. 
• Operationalizing Community Health Centers as First Referral Units (FRUs) and Primary Health 
Centers for 24X7 services; 
• Augmenting the availability of skilled manpower by means of different skill- based trainings such 
as Skilled Birth Attendance; 
• Training of MBBS Doctors in Life Saving Anesthetic Skills and Emergency Obstetric Care 
including Caesarian Section; 
• Provision of Ante-natal and Post Natal Care services; prevention and treatment of Anemia by 
supplementation with Iron and Folic Acid tablets during pregnancy and lactation; 
• Organizing Village Health & Nutrition Day at Anganwadi Centers; 
• Appointment of an Accredited Social Health Activi st (ASHA) to facilitate accessing of health care 
services by the community including pregnant women; 
• Strengthening of Health Facilities,  i.e ., District Hospitals, Community Health Centres (CHCs) 
Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and Sub Centres (S Cs), by providing them with funds including 
untied grants, Annual Maintenance Grants (AMG) and Corpus Funds to improve service 
delivery. 
Supply of foodgrains to ration card holders 
*267. SHRI VIJAYKUMAR RUPANI: Will the Mi nister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the criteria set for determining Below Poverty Line (BPL); 
(b) the steps taken by Government so that th e ration cards are only issued to genuine 
house−holds; and 
(c) the steps taken for the storage of foodgrains to ensure regular and adequate supply to 
ration card holders? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD  AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD 
PAWAR): (a) to (c) For identification of persons living below poverty line, Planning Commission 
uses a poverty line index based on per capita consumption expenditure. Poverty line is expressed in 
terms of per capita consumption expenditure needed to attain the minimum amount of calorie intake 
out of food consumed alongwith a minimum amount of non-food expenditure. The national poverty 
line at 2004-05 prices is Rs.356.30 per capita per month in rural areas and Rs.538.60 per capita per 
month in urban areas. State specific poverty lines are derived from National Poverty Line using State 
specific price indices and inter State price differentials. 

23 
Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) un der implementation since June 1997 is focused 
on below poverty line families and is operated under joint responsibility of the Government of India 
and State Governments & UT Administrations. Responsibility for identification of eligible BPL 
families as per the estimates released by the Planning Commission and issuance of ration cards to 
them rests with the State Governments and UT Administrations. 
To enable State Governments and UT Administrations to issue ration cards to genuine 
households, PDS (Control) Order, 2001 has been issued under Section 3 of Essential Commodities 
Act, 1955. Provisions under this Order mandate St ate Governments and UT Administrations to issue 
ration cards to eligible applicants and to weed out ineligible and bogus ration cards as well as bogus 
units in ration cards. 
Central Pool stocks of foodgrains meant for TPDS are stored in godowns of Food Corporation of 
India (FCI), Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC ) and State agencies by adopting scientific 
storage practices. As per allocations to States an d UTs, these agencies provide foodgrains to fair 
price shops for their timely and regular distribution to ration card holders.

*270. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND

THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD  AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD 
PAWAR): (a) to (c) It is a fact that pest infestation damages foodgrains. Some assessments have

In this connection, Government Railway Police / Lumding has registered a case vide Case Crime

Explosive Substance Act and Section 10 & 13 Unlawful Arms (Possession) Act and section 151 the

Police and RPF. 
(e) The concrete measures taken and proposes to take after the terrorist attacks are given as 
under:- 
Although the Policing on Railways is the duty of State Police through Government Railway Police, 
however, to provide better security to the traveling passengers in trains and passenger areas, the 
RPF Act, 1957 and the Railways Act, 1989 have been amended in the year 2003 to enable the 
Railways,  through  the Railway Protection Force, to effectively supplement the efforts of the State  

29 
Governments in controlling crime on the Railways and to ensure that the State Police (Government 
Railway Police) get more time to handle heinous offences such Murder, Dacoity, Robbery, Rape etc. 
including Sabotage and Train Wrecking, under the pr ovisions of Indian Penal Code, the Railways Act 
and other Raws of the land.  
After the amendment in RPF Act and Railway Act, 1257 trains are escorted by RPF daily on an 
average by deploying 3904 RPF personnel. In ad dition, 2329 trains are escorted by Government 
Railway Police by deploying 4560 personnel daily. 710 important Railway stations have been provided 
with 3898 RPF staff for access control duty.

bunkers at important stations in-Mumbai. Additional RPSF personnel have been deployed at Mumbai 
and Delhi Railway stations. Staff has been put on alert to prevent such incidents. Government 
Railway Police and State Police have also been asked to strengthen the security arrangements at 
Railway stations and in trains. 
• 96 important Railway Stations and 96 trains have been identified and deployment of RPF 
personnel for access control and escorting in trains has been augmented. 
• 140 vulnerable / sensitive Railway stations have been approved for implementation of Integrated 
Security System under Outright Purchase Model. 
• All the Railway stations of four Metro Cities i.e. Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai will be 
covered under Integrated Security System. 
• X-Ray luggage scanning machines are installed at Delhi and Chatrapati Shivaji Terminus Railway 
station Mumbai and process for procurement of more such machines is under process. 
• Electronics gadgets like CCTV, Door Frame Metal Detectors etc. have been installed at all 
important and sensitive Railway Stations. Hand Held Metal Detectors have also been provided to 
RPF personnel for frisking of passengers. Procurement of more modern security gadgets for 
installation at important Railway Stations are being done on priority. 
• Upgradation of weaponry is under process and demand for sophisticated weapons has been 
placed. 
• 3 additional Battalions of RPSF will be raised. 
• 2 RPSF Battalions will be given Commando Training and deployment of trained staff will be made 
at strategic locations. 
• On the recommendation of Norms Committee, which had been formed for fixing scales for 
procurement of modern security related equipments, Railway Board has allocated Rs. 60.76 
crores for procurement of security equipment to be used by RPF. 
• A Committee comprising officers from Railways, RPF, IB, CISF, Delhi Police and NSG was 
constituted by  the  Railway  Board  to formulate a Composite Security Plan for the Railways. The  

30 
 report submitted by the committee has been approved and is being implemented to strengthen 
security system of Railways. 
• Adequate fund will be made available under the head security for modernization and other 
expenditure in the Railways. 
• Sniffer dogs where available are utilized to ch eck explosive devices at important stations and 
trains. 
• The amendment in Railway Property (Unlawful Possession) Act 1966 has been proposed to 
control crime more effectively on the Railways. 
• Intensive publicity and public awareness campaigns alerting and educating passengers / public 
to remain vigilant against any unidentified / unclaimed suspicious objects lying and to inform 
RPF, Government Railway Police / Railway Officials available nearby about such objects. 
• Close co-ordination with GRP, State Police an d State and Central Intelligence agencies for

Ban on use of tobacco 
*274. SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN SINGH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether smokers emit cancerous smoke and pollute air; 
(b) if so, the details of measures taken to eliminate smoking; and 
(c) whether there is any proposal to ban use of tobacco in all forms? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFAR E (DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) 
There are more than 4,000 chemicals in tobacco smoke. These include a number of toxic substance 
and carcinogens or cancer causing agents viz 1,3-butadiene, Chromium VI, 2-Naphthylamine Ethyl 
benzene, 4-Aminobiphenyl Formaldehyde, 4-nitrobiphenyl Hydrazine, Acetaldehyde Methyl chloride, 
Acrolem N-Nitrosonornicotine, Aniline Nickel, Arsenic (inorganic) Nicotine, Benzene NNK, 
Benz[a]anthracene Phenol, Benzo[a]pyrene Styrene, Cadmium Toluene. 
The tobacco smoke exhaled by smokers i.e. second hand smoke is equally harmful and are 
known to cause among others:- 
1. lung cancer, heart disease, chronic lung ailments such as bronchitis and asthma 
(particularly in children), sudden infant death syndrome, acute respiratory infections, ear problems, 
and more severe asthma and low birth weight. 
2. Disease and premature death in children and adults who do not smoke. 
The tobacco smoke contains more than 4000 toxic constituents. These are poisonous gases e.g. 
hydrogen cyanide, Ammonia, Tolune, Butane and Carbon Monoxide, toxic metals e.g. Arsenic, 
Cadmium, Chromium and Lead and Cancer causing chemicals such as Vinyl Chloride Benzene, 
Formaldehyde and Polonium. 
Active smoking ( i.e. the smoke to which the smoker is exposed) leads to cancers of various 
organs such a lungs, larynx, liver, stomach, pancreas, kidney, cervix (women), urethra and 
bladder, leukemia (blood cancer) and other diseas e such as stroke, cataract, diminished health, 
coronary heart disease and chronic lung disease. 
There is scientific evidence to prove that the persons who are exposed to second hand smoke 
(SHS) or Environmental Tobacco Smoke (ETS) get disease and adverse health effects such as lung 
cancer and heart disease in adults and SIDS (S udden Infant Death Syndrome) exacerbation of 
asthma, acute and chronic lung disease and middle ear disease in children. 
The Government of India has enacted a comp rehensive Tobacco Control Act called "The 
Cigarettes and other Tobacco Products (Prohibition  of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and 
Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003" in May, 2003. The main objective of the 
act is to discourage the consumption of ciga rettes and other tobacco products. The specific 
provisions contained in the Act include: 
1. Ban on smoking in public places. (Section-4) 
2. Ban on direct/indirect advertisement of tobacco products. (Section-5) 

33 
3. Ban on sale of tobacco products to children below 18 years. (Section-6a) 
4. Ban on sale of tobacco products within 100 yards of the educational  
  institution. (Section-6b) 
5. Specified health warnings on  tobacco products. (Section-7) 
The section-4 of the said Act prohibits smoking in public places, thereby protecting the non-
smokers from second hand smoke/environmental toba cco smoke. The Ministry of Health has issued 
guidelines to the State Governments/ Departments to implement the smoke-free rules. 
Further, the pilot phase of National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP) has also been 
launched in 2007-08 in 18 districts of 9 States. Th e NTCP envisages building capacity of the State 
Governments in the effective enforcement of Anti Tobacco Laws and bringing about greater 
awareness about the ill effects of tobacco. 
It is expected that the initiatives of the Government, in bringing about greater awareness of the 
harm effects of tobacco & strict enforcement of th e anti-tobacco laws will protect the non-smokers 
& also progressively reduce the demand of tobacco products in India.

Procurement of anti-rabbies vaccine 
*279. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
 SHRIMATI SHOBHNA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be phased to state: 
(a) whether the Centre Government hospitals in the Capital are procuring poor quality anti-
rabbies vaccine for patients; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that most developed nations have discontinued the use of equine 
serum, being outdated; and 
(d) if so, the reasons of continuing outdat ed treatment of patients bitten by dogs? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) 
In  so  far  as Central Government hospitals are concerned, Anti-Rabies Vaccines (ARV) of standard  

37 
quality are procured. These biological (vaccine/serum) whether indigenously produced or imported 
cannot be marketed unless their quality is certified by the Central Drug Laboratory at Kasauli. There 
has been no complaint about the quality of these vaccines. 
Anti-rabies immunoglobulin is life saving medi cine for passive immunization and provides the 
immediate availability of neutralizing antibodies at the site of bite to tide over the initial phase of 
infection before the patient begins to produce his or her own antibodies after anti-rabies vaccination. 
Hence, national and international (WHO) guidelines recommend administration of immunoglobulin in 
all category III exposures and category II exposure in immune compromised patients. 
Equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG) is one of the products available for passive immunization. 
ERIG currently manufactured are potent, highly purified, safe and not expensive. These are used in 
the countries where rabies continues to be major public health problem.

Criteria for fixing minimum support price 
2019. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any specific criteria to fix the minimum support price for rice and wheat; 
(b) whether any minimum support price has been fixed for oilseeds and onion; and 

46 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): 
(a) The Government decides on the Minimum Support Price (MSP) for various agricultural 
commodities, including paddy and wheat, taki ng into account the recommendations of the 
Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CAC P), the views of State Governments and Central 
Ministries as well as such other relevant factors which are considered important for fixation of support 
prices. The CACP, while formulating its recommendations on price policy considers a number of 
important factors which includes cost of production, changes in input prices, input/output price 
parity, trends in market prices, demand and supply situation, inter-crop price parity, effect on 
industrial cost structure, effect on general price le vel, effect on cost of living, international market 
price situation and parity between prices paid and prices received by the farmers. 
The cost of cultivation/production taken into account includes all paid out costs, such as, those 
incurred on account of hired human labour, bullock labour/machine labour (both hired and owned) 
and rent paid for leased in land besides cash and kind expenses on use of material inputs like seeds, 
fertilizers, manures, irrigation charges including cost of diesel/electricity for operation of pump sets, 
etc. Besides, cost of production includes imputed value of wages of family labour and rent for owned 
land. The cost also covers depreciation of farm  machinery and buildings. As such, the cost of 
production covers not only actual expenses in cash  and kind but also imputed value of owned assets 
including land and family labour. 
(b) and (c) MSPs of oilseeds are fixed alongwith the fixation of MSPs of Kharif and Rabi crops. 
MSP of onion is not fixed. However, the Government implements the Market Intervention Scheme 
(MIS) on the request of a State/UT Government fo r procurement of agricultural and horticultural 
commodities generally perishable in nature, includ ing onion. The MIS is implemented in order to 
protect the growers of horticultural commodities from making distress sale in the event of bumper 
crop during the peak arrival period when prices tend to fall below economic levels. Losses, if any, 
incurred by the procuring agencies are shared  between Central Government and the concerned 
State Government on 50:50 basis (75:25 in case of No rth Eastern States), Profit, if any, earned by 
the procuring agencies is retained by them.

†2022. SHRI PRABHAT JHA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that cases of suicides by farmers in different parts of the country are 
increasing inspite of announcement of Rehabilitation package and waiving of loans; 
(b) if so, the State-wise details with regard to cases of suicides came to the knowledge of the

Maharashtra, Karnataka and Kerala. Some cases of su icides by farmers were also reported from the 
States of Gujarat, Punjab and Tamil Nadu. A Statement indicating the number of suicides by farmers 
as reported by the State Governments is enclosed. As reported by the State Governments, the 
causes of suicide by farmers are broadly crop failure, indebtedness, drought and social and 
economic insecurity. To address the problem of suicide by farmers, the Government of India  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

54 
approved a rehabilitation package of Rs. 16978.69 crore for 31 Districts in the four States of Andhra 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Kerala reporting comparatively higher number of suicides by 
farmers. The package being implemented includes  both immediate and me dium term measures. 
Measures taken by Government include waiver and debt relief for farmers announced in the Union 
Budget 2008-09 to address the problem of indebtedness of farmers. The scheme has been 
implemented by Ministry of Finance benefiting about 3.68 crore of farmers with total amount of waiver 
and relief amounting to about Rs.65318 crore. Meas ures taken by Government for revitalisation of 
agriculture sector include launching of new schemes, namely, National Food Security Mission to 
improve production and productivity of foodgrains and Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana with an objective 
to improve growth rate of agriculture and allied se ctor and to incentives the States so as to increase 
public investment in agriculture and allied sector.

Contract farming 
2028. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has formulated a Working Group on contract farming; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the important decision taken by the Working Group; 
(d) the details of crops and regions associated with contract farming along with the benefits 
likely to accrue therefrom; 
(e) whether there is any proposal for State regulation, intermediation and monitoring of 
contract farming; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Planning Commission of India had set up a Working Group of the Sub-Committee of 
the National Development Council on Agriculture and Related Issues relating to Marketing Reforms, 
Contract Farming and Agro-Processing Sector unde r the Chairmanship of the Chief Minister of 
Punjab. The Terms of Reference of this Working Group relating to the Contract Farming were to 
suggest the current status of contract farming with a view to identify the lacunae and suggest the 
appropriate models; to suggest an appropriate legal framework with dispute settlement mechanism 
and compensation procedures; to device a system for providing services including quality inputs, 
technical knowledge, finance and price fixation for the marketable produce; to suggest a system of 
identifying the technologies to be introduced for contract farming with a provision of compensation 
for any under-performance or failure of the technologies introduced by the sponsors; to suggest 
legal, institutional and / or financial measures required for encouraging contract farming 
arrangements between the farmers and the agro-processing industry / exporters; and to identify 
area specific agriculture commodities suitable for Contract Farming for selected agro climatic 
conditions. 
(c) The Report of the Working Group was disc ussed in the meeting of the Sub-Committee of 
NDC on Agriculture and Related Issues on 18.04.2007 and subsequently its recommendations were 
considered by the National Development Council in its 53rd Meeting on 29.05.2007. NDC has 
resolved in the meeting that State Governments would encourage development of modern markets 
by completing the process of amending their Agri cultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) Acts 
and notify the Rules thereunder and would also encourage development of linkages to markets 
through a variety of instruments including cooperat ive of farmers, contract farming and other means 
preferred by the States. 
(d) The details of crops and regions associated with contract farming along with the benefits 
likely to accrue therefrom are not being maintained by the Ministry of Agriculture. 

65 
(e) and (f) The Model Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act circulated by the Ministry 
of Agriculture to the States/ Union Territories (U Ts) in 2003 for implementi ng marketing reforms has 
provisions for the registration of contract farm ing sponsors and recording of contract farming 
agreements with the Agricultural Produce Marketing Committee (APMC) or a prescribed authority 
under the Act; protection of title or rights of the farmers over the land under such contracts; dispute 
settlement mechanism and a model draft agreement suggesting various terms and conditions. By 
now, relevant provisions have been made by 18  State Governments / UTs in their respective APMC 
Acts for providing a legal framework to contract fa rming. In seven States / UTs, there are no APMC 
Acts, therefore, there is no regulation of contract fa rming in such States / UTs.  To help States in the 
formulation of Rules in this regard, the Ministry of Agriculture has also circulated a set of Model 
APMC Rules to them for adoption. The Model Act circulated by the Ministry is suggestive in nature, 
and since agriculture is a State subject, it is for the State Governments to decide on the 
implementation, intermediation and monitoring of the contract farming arrangements in their States.

2034. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal to modernize the infrastructure for fisheries sector; 
(b) if so, the details thereof including the sector/areas for immediate modernization; 
(c) the details of the estimated cost of modernization of the infrastructure, State wise and 
category-wise; and 
(d) the steps taken for pathogen free shrimp seed and facilities for cleanliness and hygiene for 
export up to the requirement of European and other countries standard, in detail, State-wise and 
category wise, as on date? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) to 
(c) The Ministry of Agriculture, Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying and Fisheries under the 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA) 
and National Fisheries Development Board (NFDB) provide financial assistance and technical 
support to State Governments, Union Territories (UT), Port Trusts, Fisheries Corporations/ 
Federations, Fishermen Cooperatives etc. for development and modernization of infrastructure in the 
fisheries sector such as (i) construction of new fishing harbours and fish landing centres, (ii) 
modernization of existing fishing harbours and fish landing centres, (iii) establishment of post harvest

establishment of hatcheries, (vi) acquisition of reso urce specific fishing vessels, (vii) construction of

other implementing agencies subject to viability of the project and overall budgetary allocation.

(iii) Supply of disease free nauplii to farmers through the RGCA production facility. 
(iv) Setting up disease diagnostic laboratories for identifying pathogens through polymerase Chain

(c) and (d) The inflation under food articles during the 1st quarter (April-June) of 2008 was

taken by the Government:- 
(i) Reducing import duty to zero for rice, wheat , pulses, edible oils (crude), maize, butter and 
ghee. 
(ii) Reducing import duty on refined, hydrogenated and vegetable oils to 7.5%. 
(iii) Banning exports of non-basmati rice, wheat, selected edible oils and pulses. 
(iv) Imposing stock limit orders in case of paddy, rice, wheat, edible oils and oilseeds. 
(v) Reduction on import duty of skimmed milk powder from 15% to 5%. 
(vi) Using Minimum Export Price (MEP) to regulate export of onion and basmati rice. 
(vii) Maintaining Central Issue Price (CIP) for rice and wheat for Below Poverty Line (BPL) and 
Antyodaya Anna Yojna (AYY). 
(viii) Reduction in the prices of petrol and diesel respectively by Rs. 5 and Rs. 2 per liter.

2037. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has any proposal to enact a law to protect the shrinking agricultural 
land in the country especially due to industrialization and acquisition of land for Special Economic 
Zones; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the shrinking cultivable land could lead to heavy shortage of foodgrains thereby 
threatening food security; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the remedial steps taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): 
(a) and (b) As per the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India, Land falls under the purview of 
State Government,  therefore,  it for the States to bring suitable legislation to protect the diversion of

sown area" in the country has remained approximately the same  i.e. 141 million ha due to various 
interventions made by the Government.

New investment policy in the fertilizer sector 
2051. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government is contemplating to formulate a new investment policy in fertilizer 
sector; 
(b) if so, the salient features thereof; 

90 
(c) the extent to which the aforesaid policy is likely to bridge the gap between consumption 
and domestic production; and 
(d) the time by when the new policy is likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI B.K. 
HANDIQUE): (a) to (d) The Government has already finalized and announced a policy for New 
Investments in Urea sector on 4th September 2008. Th e New Investment Policy aims at increase in 
indigenous production capacity through revamp, expansion, revival of existing urea units and setting 
up of Greenfield projects. The policy is likely to substantially bridge the gap in next five years between 
the consumption and indigenous production of urea subject to confirmed and adequate availability of 
gas at reasonable prices for the fertilizer sector. The salient features of the new investment policy are 
as under:- 
1. The policy is based on Import Parity Price (I PP) benchmark with floor and ceiling price of USD 
250 PMT and USD 425 PMT respectively. 
2. Revamp project: Any improvement in capacity of existing  plants through investment upto Rs. 
1000 crore, in the existing train of ammonia-urea production will be treated as revamp of existing 
units. The additional urea from the revamp of existing units will be recognized at 85% of Import 
Parity Price with the floor and ceiling price as indicated above. 
3. Expansion projects:  Setting up of a new ammonia-urea plant (a separate new ammonia-urea 
train) in the premises of the existing fertilizer plants, utilizing some of the common utilities will 
qualify for being treated as expansion project. Th e investment should exceed a minimum limit of 
Rs.3000 crore. The urea from the expansion of exis ting units will be recognized at 90% of IPP, 
with the floor and ceiling price as indicated above. 
4. Revival/Brownfield projects: The urea from the revived units of Hindustan Fertilizer Corporation 
Limited (HFCL) and Fertilizer Corporation of Indi a Limited (FCIL) will be recognized at 95% of 
IPP with prescribed floor & ceiling price, if the revival of closed units takes placed in public 
sector. 
5. Greenfield projects:  The pricing of Greenfield projects will be decided based on a bidding 
process which will be for a discount over IPP, after firming up of the location (States) of the 
proposed new plants. 
6. Gas transportation charges:  An additional gas transportation cost will be paid to units 
undertaking expansion and revival on the basis of actuals (upto 5.2 Gcal per MT of urea) as 
decided by the Regulator(Gas) subject to a maximum ceiling of USD 25 per MT of urea. 
7. Allocation of Gas: Only non-APM gas will be considered for the new investment in urea sector. 
8. Coal gasification based Urea Projects: The Coal gasification based urea projects will also be 
treated  on  par  with a revival or a Greenfield project as the case may be. In addition, any other  

91 
 incentives or tax benefits as provided by Government for encouraging coal gasification 
technology will also be extended to these projects. 
9. Joint Ventures abroad: The Joint Venture projects abroad in gas rich countries are also proposed 
to be encouraged through firm offtake contracts with pricing decided on the basis of prevailing 
market conditions and in mutual consultation with the joint venture company. However, the 
principle for deciding upon the maximum price will be the price achieved under Greenfield 
projects or 95% of IPP as proposed for revival projects (in absence of any Greenfield projects) 
with a cap of USD 405 CIF India per MT and a floor of USD 225 CIF India per MT (inclusive of 
handling and bagging costs). 
10. Time period for proposed investment policy: Only those revamp projects which start production 
of additional capacities within four years of notification of the new policy would qualify for the 
dispensation recommended above. Similarly production from expansion and revival (brownfield) 
units that come about within five years of no tification of the new policy would qualify for 
dispensation provided in the policy. If the production does not come through within the stipulated 
time period, such brownfield projects will be treated similar to a Greenfield projects wherein price 
will be decided through limited bidding options. The time period for setting up of new Joint 
Ventures would also be five years under the new investment policy.

amount of Factomfos for the last two years, month-wise, and category-wise;

HANDIQUE): (a) to (d) Urea is the only fertilizer which is under partial movement and distribution 
control of the Government. Union Government ensures availability of urea at State level. State 
Governments are responsible for its distribution within  the State. All other fertilizers like DAP, MOP, 
SSP and NPK etc. are decontrolled / de-canaliz ed since 1992. The monthly supply plans for 
decontrolled fertilizers are drawn by manufacturers / importers of these fertilizers in consultation with 
the State Government. Therefore, the availability of Phosphatic and Potassic fertilizers is decided by 
the market forces of demand and supply.

Factomfos is complex fertilizer, manufactured by M/s. Fertilizer and Chemicals Travancore

shortage of raw material and also due to the wo rking capital problems. FACT intends to maximize 
their production of Factomfos during the forthcomin g season in order to cater to the need of the

Recovery of penalty from erring pharma companies 
2053. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether drug regulator needs power as Government had imposed Rs.1627 crores penalty 
on companies but recovery has been only Rs.130 crores till October; 
(b) if so, what are the main reasons of low recovery; 
(c) what are the steps being taken to recover all the amount; 
(d) whether norms for sale of medical devices likely by February, 2009; 
(e) whether Government is also setting up outlets to sell drugs at cheaper prices; and 
(f) whether price control is necessary in drug market and what are the efforts being made in 
this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI B.K. 
HANDIQUE): (a) to (c) Since the inception of Na tional Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in 
August 1997, NPPA has raised a total demand of Rs. 1830.57 crores (up to 15.12.08) for recovery 
towards overcharged amount, under the provisions of Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO, 
1995)  read  with  Essential  Commodities  Act,  1955.  NPPA  has recovered Rs.139.54 crores so far  

95 
(upto 15.12.08) from defaulting companies. NPPA continues to take appropriate action regularly for 
recovery of the overcharged amount. In some cases the recovery is affected where the companies 
have approached the Hon'ble Courts and the cases are still sub-judice. 
(d) At present there is no proposal under consideration of the Government to regulate the sale 
of medical devices. However, a guideline specifying requirements for manufacturing, import of 
medical devices is being prepared. The time frame for the same is yet to be finalised. 
(e) Yes, Sir. Government has decided to open  "Jan Aushadhi" generic drug stores in the 
country depending upon the financial assistance and other support offered by respective State 
Governments. The first generic drug store in the name of "Jan Aushadhi" has been opened at Civil 
Hospital, Amritsar (Punjab) on 25.11.2008. 
(f) Price control mechanism of the Government is based on the economic criteria aimed at 
controlling monopolies in the mass consumption drugs.  The Government believes that in most of the 
cases competition is not able to control the prices and consequently there is need to exercise price 
control. Presently, price control on drugs is done under the provisions of Drugs (Price Control) 
Order, 1995. To strengthen the price control mechan ism a Draft National Pharmaceuticals Policy was 
submitted before the Cabinet for its approval. The Cabinet considered the Policy in its meeting held 
on 11-1-2007 and decided that the matter may, in the first instance, be considered by a Group of 
Ministers (GOM). GOM has since been constituted and has held four meetings so far. GOM is yet to 
make its recommendations to the Cabinet.

Perishing of foodgrains and vegetables due to shortage of cold storages 
†2055. MS. SUSHILA TIRIYA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of foodgrains, pulses and vege tables etc. that perishes in transit before 
reaching to consumer from the field of farmers; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that 30 per cent of foods and vegetables go waste due to shortage 
of cold stores; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that out of total wastage from 15 to 30 per cent go wastes due to 
weeds and improper pesticides; 
(d) if so, whether Government would take any step to provide sufficient information and 
training to farmers in this regard; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) to (c) On wastage of foodgrains and vegetables due to 
various factors, only sporadic survey/study data is available. Government of India constituted a 
committee under the Chairmanship of Dr. V.C. Panse, the then member of Planning Commission for 
assessment of Post harvest losses in foodgrains. As per Panse Committee report (1966), total post 
harvest losses in foodgrains have been assessed as 9.33% out of which losses during transportation 
were estimated as 0.15%. 
The percentage of foodgrains, pulses losses on an average ranges from 8 to 10 per cent and 10 
to 30 per cent in respect of vegetables. The number of cold storages has increased from 4541 
(December 2003) to 5316 (December, 2007) which helps to reduce wastage of food and vegetables. 
(d) to (e) Government is promoting technology developed by Central Institute of Post Harvest 
"Engineering and Technology (CIPHET) Ludhiana and All India Coordinated Research Project 
(AICRP) on Post Harvest Management which are being demonstrated to farmers. Awareness and 
training programme on Post harvest management is also organized under the Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme on National Horticulture Mission for vegeta bles and also by National Horticulture Board an 
apex organization under Ministry of Agriculture. 
Integrated policy for import of wheat and edible oils 
2056. SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that need for formulat ing an integrated policy on importing wheat and 
edible oil is being felt; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 

104 
(c) the efforts being made by Government to make adequate quantity of wheat and mustard 
seeds available to States under Food Safety Mission scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) The Government is continuously 
monitoring the food situation in the country and poli cies regarding import of wheat and edible oil are 
being accordingly, formulated from the time to time, keeping in view the domestic production, 
consumption requirements, domestic and international prices, etc. 
(c) A Centrally Sponsored Scheme on "National Food Security Mission" has been launched in 
view of the resolution of National Development Council (NDC) to launch a Food Security Mission in 
the country to enhance the production of rice, wheat and pulses by 10, 8, and 2 million tonnes, 
respectively by the end of XI plan. 
The Mission aims at increasing production of rice, wheat and pulses through area expansion and 
productivity enhancement, restoring soil fertility and productivity, creating employment opportunities, 
and improving farm level economy to restore confidence of farmers of targeted districts. 
Under NFSM, demonstration of improved production technology, distribution of quality seeds of 
High Yield Varieties (HYVs) and hybrids, popularization of newly released varieties is done.

Export of wheat 
†2058. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
    SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a proposal to export wheat in excess of consumption 
requirement of the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the quantity of wheat available for export; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that there would be less production of wheat at international level 
next year; and 
(d) if so, the assessment in this regard, and whether India's requirement of wheat in 2009 has 
been estimated to be met by domestic resources? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC

wheat stock in Central Pool, it has been decided by  the Government to allow export of upto 20 lakh

Affairs will make payment to FCI, at economic cost.

global production of wheat for 2008-09 is 683 million tonnes, as against 610 million tonnes in 2007-
08.

Storage facilities for foodgrains 
2059. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that public sector companies like Food Corporation of India (FCI) and 
Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) do not have sufficient number of godowns to store 
foodgrains; 
(b) if so, the total number of godowns and the storage capacity of each godown; 
(c) whether it is a fact that huge quantity of foodgrains stored in the godowns of FCI and CWC 
was lost due to poor storage and highly deficient management; 
(d) if so, the loss of foodgrains during last three years, year-wise; and 
(e) the steps taken by the Central Government to provide better storage facilities in the 
godowns of FCI and CWC? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) No, Sir. There is sufficient storage capacity 
available with Food Corporation of India (FCI) and Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) to store 
foodgrains. FCI have 1549 godowns with total st orage capacity of 243.40 lakh tonnes (Owned & 
hired/Covered & CAP) against which total stocks held as on 31.10.2008 was 147.72 lakh tonnes. 
CWC have 492 godowns with total storage capacity of 98.15 lakh MTs against which stock held on 
31.10.2008 •was 73.95 lakh MTs. 
(b) The information is being collected and will be laid on the Table of the House. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. All godowns of FCI have been constructed as per ISI Code 607.1071 and 
likewise, CWC is storing foodgrains in its warehous es by adopting scientific methods. All godowns 
are being maintained properly. Hence, storage loss in FCI and CWC godowns is not attributed to 
poor storage and deficient management. 
(e) Steps taken by the Central Government to provide better storage facilities in the godowns 
of FCI and CWC are:- 
(i) All godowns are constructed as per specifi cation and foodgrains ar e stored by adopting 
scientific storage practices. 
(ii) Adequate dunnage material, fumigation covers and chemicals are provided in all the godowns. 
(iii) Prophylactic and curative treatments are carr ied out regularly and timely for the control of 
insects and pests. 

107 
(iv) Foodgrains in 'cover and plinth' (CAP) stor age are stored on elevated plinths and wooden 
crates are used as dunnage material. Stacks are properly covered with specifically fabricated 
low density black polythene water proof covers and tied with nylon ropes/nets. 
(v) Regular inspections of the stocks/godowns are undertaken by qualified and trained staff. 
(vi) The principle of 'First In First Out' (FIFO) is adopted to the extent possible so as to avoid 
longer storage of foodgrains in the godowns. 
(vii) Only covered wagons are used for movement of foodgrains so as to avoid damages during 
transit.

Governments. The Government of India, carries out procurement of foodgrains for the TPDS, their

Citizens' Charter, monthly certification of delivery of foodgrains to fair price shops and their 
distribution to ration card holders, and taking up publicity-cum-awareness campaign have been

Mortality rates in the country 
2080. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: 
 DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that child mortality rate in India is higher than Bangladesh 
and Nepal; 
(b) whether out of all the States five States have  recorded higher mortality rates, and if so, the 
details thereof; 
(c) what are the schemes and programmes under his Ministry to minimize the infant mortality 
rate and for the development of children and budgetary allocations for each scheme; and 
(d) what is the State-wise performance and how his Ministry monitors such programmes? 

129 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) 
The child mortality rate in India for the year 2006 is 17.0 per thousand live births. The year-wise 
figures and State-wise figure are given in the Statement (See below). 
The States with highest child mortality are Madhya Pradesh 24.3 per 1000 live births, Uttar 
Pradesh 23.9 per 1000 live births, Rajasthan, 22.4 pe r 1000 live births, Orissa 22.0 per 1000 live 
births, and Assam 19.7 per 1000 live births. 
As per The State of World's children 2008 report of UNICEF, the under five mortality for year 2006 
for India is 76 per 1000 live births, for Bangladesh is 69 per 1000 live births and for Nepal is 59 per 1000 
live births. 
The under five mortality rate (the probability of a child dying between birth and exactly five years 
of age) used by UNICEF in its report is different fr om the child mortality rate (the probability of a child 
dying between first and the fifth birthday) used by Sample Registration System, Registrar General of 
India. 
The National Rural Health Mission, launched in April, 2005 for a period of 7 years (2005 to 2012) 
is an umbrella initiative which covers the existing initiatives of Reproductive and Child Health (RCH II) 
also. The interventions under NRHM are aimed at improving the efficiency of the RCH II programme 
and accelerate the reduction of Infant Mortality Rate (IMR). NRHM facilitates simultaneous action on 
collateral determinants of health like water, sanitation, education, nutrition, etc. 
A major initiative is implementation of the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood 
Illnesses (IMNCI) strategy, which adopts a holistic approach to the management of the commonest 
causes of neonatal and childhood mortality – sepsis acute respiratory infections diarrhoea, measles 
and malaria, all compounded by malnutrition. In addi tion, thrust is being given to ensure institutional 
deliveries and trained health personnel on essential newborn care so that skilled attendance at birth is 
available and all newborns receive specialized care. Efforts to deliver new born and child care, both 
facility based as well as home based, are being made. Micronutrient supplementation with Vitamin A, 
Iron Folic Acid and Zinc and Infant and Young Child  Nutrition are being stressed. Immunization is one 
of the major thrust areas of the ongoing Reproductive & Child Health Programme. 
Funds are allocated to the States as Flexi pool  as per their requirements projected in State 
Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs). Subsequently  States have full freedom to allocate funds 
provided under flexi pool for various activities includ ing child health. Budget Estimate of Flexi pool is 
given in the Statement-II (See below). 
The progress is good. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has an elaborate monitoring and 
evaluation system for monitoring the progress of  its programmes and evaluating its impact. The 
National programmes are monitored through external surveys and stringent internal monitoring by the 
National Rural Health Mission.

Kidney Rackets 
†2081. SHRI AJAY SINGH CHAUTALA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in the recent past  a racket of kidney transplantation was unearthed 
where in kidneys of a large number of poor people were removed; 
(b) whether foreigners were also involved in it; 
(c) whether Government has taken any measure to check such immoral activities; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, whether Government will take stringent measures in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. A kidney  scam in Gurgaon, Haryana came to notice 
through media on 25.01.2008. It was alleged that mo re than 500 kidney transplants have taken place

Kumar, Dr. K.K. Aggarwal. Sale/ purchase of human organs is already prohibited under 
Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994. Appropriate authorities established under this Act are 
responsible and empowered to check the illegal activities of human organs trafficking. A Statement 
showing the details received from the State Governments is enclosed.

Alcohol Control Policy 
2083. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has decided to launch a national policy for alcohol control; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the suggestions from experts and scientists have been invited for the proper 
formation of the alcohol control policy; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the details of the other steps Government prop ose to take to ensure that policy on alcohol 
control is implemented and the youths who are addict to it can be saved? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) The policy with regard to sale and distribution of alcohol is 
within the purview of the State Governments. Therefore, the efforts made to contain the damage 
done by alcoholism vary from State to State. Apar t from this, clinical care, building awareness, 
counseling and rehabilitation is made available through de-addiction centres and counseling centres 
run/funded by the Government. 
(c) to (e) The need to frame a policy on alco hol control has been discussed with the experts 
and scientists. To make an effective national policy there is need to introduce legislative changes, 
identify national structures responsible, develop quality data system, to have Central Law on alcohol 
instead of State specific laws, uniform policy and taxation in all States and UT, increase minimum 
legal drinking from 18-21. Views of the State Governments and UTs are to be obtained in this regard.

Proper care to girl child 
2085. SHRIMATI SURPRIYA SULE: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Prime Minister has urged every St ate to step forward to empower the girl child; 
(b) if so, whether the National Family Health Survey-III has found that in the five years 
preceding the survey, 44 per cent of urban and 80 per cent of the rural respondents had opted for 
prenatal ultrasound tests; 
(c) if so, whether the Prime Minister has urged upon the States to take urgent steps to see that 
children born are given proper treatment; 
(d) the suggestions made by the Pr ime Minister in this regard; and 
(e) to what extent the Union Government and the States have agreed to implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFAR E (DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (e) 
On the occasion of the national level meet on 'S ave the Girl Child' held at New Delhi on 28.4.2008, 
the hon'ble Prime Minister of India urged, inter alia,  for a concerned and multi pronged societal 
action to address the several contributing factors in the precament of the Indian girl child. There was 
need to strengthen legislative enforcement, basic health care and nutrition and reorient national 
literacy and school education programmes to give greater focus, to women and the girl child. 
Leaders of civil society, particularly the religious leaders needed to be mobilized for a nationwide 
campaign for ending all types of discrimination ag ainst our women built into our societal structure. 
The hon'ble Prime Minister exhorted every citizen to step forward and help in empowering the girl 
child in every possible way. 
The National Population Policy (NPP) 2000, the National Health Policy, 2002 and the Tenth Five 
Year Plan (2002-2007) have laid down the goals for maternal and child health initiatives which are 
also a part of the Millennium Development Goals, to which India is a signatory. The National Rural 
Health Mission (NRHM) goal is to reduce Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) to 30 by 2012. 
The ongoing Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme-II under National Rural Health 
Mission (NRHM) comprehensively integrates interventions to improve child health and was initiated 
to address each of the major factors contributing to high IMR and under-five mortality. 
(b) The National Family Health Survey-Ill found that the percentage of all pregnancies in the five 
years preceding the survey for which an ultrasound test was done in terms of residence is 44.0% in 
urban areas and 16.3% in rural areas.

Malnutrition 
†2090. SHRI SATYAVRAT CHATURVEDI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that 46 per cent of the children in the country are suffering 
from malnutrition and 47 per cent of the children are under weight; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that there has been stunted physical growth of 38 per cent of 
children; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

138 
(c) whether the future generation will be weak due to weak children and this would adversely 
affect the economic progress of the country; and 
(d) if so, the steps being taken by Go vernment to improve this situation? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) 
As per the National Family Health Survey (NFHS)-III (2005-06), in India 42.5% children under the 
age of five years are underweight and 48% are stunted. 
(c) Malnutrition during pregnancy can result in low birth weight and small for date babies. 
These children are more prone to malnutrition during all phases of life. Thus a vicious cycle of 
malnutrition is perpetuated. Further, malnutrition reduces capacity to work which affects the 
productivity in the country. 
(d) The remedial steps being taken, by the Government to check problem of malnutrition are 
the promotion of early initiation of breastfeeding; exclusive breast feeding for the first six months of 
life; promotion of complementary feeding from the age of six months onwards with continuation of 
breast feeding up to two years of age; and counseling of mothers and care givers for healthy feeding 
practices in children. 
A National Nutrition Policy has been adopted by the Ministry of Women and Child Development in 
1993 and a National Plan of Action for Nutrition (1995) is being implemented. The National Nutrition 
Mission has been set up by the nodal Ministry for Nutrition i.e. Ministry of Women & Child 
Development. 
The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare implements the Reproductive and Child Health 
Programme throughout the country under National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) which includes: 
• Specific programmes to manage micronutrient de ficiencies of Vitamin A and Iron & Folic Acid 
through supplementation. Vitamin A is supplemented for children from the age of nine months till 
the age of 5 years and Iron & Folic Acid supplementation is provided for infants, preschool 
children, adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women. 
• The National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Co ntrol Programme (NIDDCP) is implemented by 
provision of iodized salt throughout the country. 
Spending on healthcare 
†2091. SHRI SHIVANAND TIWARI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that an average family in the country has to spend 6.7 per cent of its 
annual income on medical purposes; 
(b) if so, the facts in this regard and whether it is  also a fact that this expenditure on health is 
due to expensive medical system; 
(c) if not, the reaction of Government thereto and whether health insurance system can help to 
get rid of this expensive medical system; and 
(d) if so, the scheme of Government for health insurance system? 

139 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) As per data made available in National Sample Survey 
Organization (NSSO) 61st round (2004-05) 7% of total consumer expenditure in rural India and 5% 
in urban India is on Medical expenses. 
The report of the Task Force on Medical Education states that the private sector provides 58% 
of hospitals, 29% of the beds and 81% of the doctors. 77% of the OPD cases in rural areas and 
80% in the urban areas are being serviced by the private sector in the country. As per Reports of the 
60th Round of NSSO, the average expenditure per hospitalization in Government in rural area is 
Rs.3,238/-while the cost in private is Rs.7,408/-. Th is high degree of reliance on the private sector 
has led to relatively high cost of health care. The Government of India has therefore launched 
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) with the ai m to provide affordable care by strengthening the 
public health system and thereby rectifying this an omaly. Health Insurance is not the only, but one of 
the many interventions under NRHM which seek to reduce the high out of pocket expenditure that 
households incur in times of seeking hospitalized care. 
NRHM has adopted health insurance for BPL population of the country. The cost of the annual 
premium up to 75%, subject to a maximum of Rs.300/- per BPL Family is borne by Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare. 
A Framework for developing health insurance programme (some suggestions for the States) 
have been developed and the Government has advised the State/UT Governments to prepare Health 
Insurance models as per their local needs to be run on pilot basis. 
The State Government of Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Mizoram have sent 
proposals for pilot projects under NRHM. 
Further, another scheme, Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana has been introduced by the Ministry 
of Labour for the BPL Family of workers of Unorganized Sector in April 2008. The premium up to 
75%, subject to maximum of Rs.565/- per annum per BPL Family of workers of Unorganized Sector 
shall be borne by Ministry of Labour for a Insurance Cover of Rs.30,000/- on floater basis.

persons whose standard of living is lower than of those whose standard living is high;

(c) The incidence of tuberculosis disease is esti mated from ARTI (Annual Risk of Tuberculosis

year 2000-2003. As per latest ARTI survey, the incide nce of tuberculosis is estimated to be 168 per

However, there are few studies conducted in India on a limited scale which have shown that 
prevalence of tuberculosis is about 3-4 times higher in the lower economic strata.

incidence of TB is concerned, as per latest WHO Global Report-2008, India ranks at 17th position

persons who are infected with TB bacilli do not develop TB disease. There is a 10% life time risk that

2100. SHRI N. BALAGANGA: Will the Minister of  HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Indian population would overtake China by 2050; 
(b) whether Government has taken any steps to control population explosion;

149
